Turn 1 of 4 — read-back. Do not write any program JSON in this turn.

You are going to turn a protocol into a Rhylthyme program: parallel **tracks** of sequential **steps**, each with a duration and a start trigger, that one person follows against a live clock.

Plan this as a Rhylthyme protocol and deliver a live timeline: Colony PCR Screen with a Diagnostic Gel for eight clones, one gel
Resource limits: one thermocycler, one microcentrifuge, one microwave, one gel rig, one transilluminator, one operator.
No finishing time was given; finish as early as the work allows.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Colony PCR Screen with a Diagnostic Gel

Eight candidate clones are screened by PCR and the products are run on a single agarose gel. The bench has one thermocycler, one microcentrifuge, a microwave, one gel rig and one transilluminator, and one person runs the whole thing. The cycling block is long enough to cast and set the gel while it runs, so start the agarose partway through the run rather than waiting for the machine to finish.

Part 1: Reaction setup
1. Thaw the primers, dNTPs and 10× buffer on ice; 15 minutes. Keep the polymerase in the cold block until the last moment.
2. Assemble a 25 µL master mix on ice for eight reactions plus one spare; 10 minutes of pipetting.
3. Aliquot 25 µL into eight strip tubes, add 1 µL of each colony suspension and spin them down for 30 seconds in the microcentrifuge; 5 minutes.

Part 2: Cycling
4. Load the strip tubes into the thermocycler and start the program; 3 minutes.
5. Run 95 °C for 3 minutes, then 35 cycles of 95 °C for 30 seconds, 58 °C for 30 seconds and 72 °C for 45 seconds, then a final 72 °C for 5 minutes. The block reports 1 hour 50 minutes.

Part 3: Agarose gel
6. Twenty-five minutes into the cycling run, weigh 1.0 g of agarose into 100 mL of 1× TAE and microwave for 3 minutes, swirling once, until no lens of undissolved agarose is left.
7. Cool the flask on the bench for 12 minutes, until it is comfortable to hold.
8. Add 5 µL of DNA stain, pour the gel into the casting tray and seat the 10-well comb; 3 minutes.
9. Let the gel set for 35 minutes at room temperature. Do not rush this; a soft gel tears at the wells.
10. Remove the comb and place the gel in the rig under 1× TAE; 2 minutes.

Part 4: Run and read
11. Ten minutes after the gel is poured to set, thaw the 100 bp ladder and mix it with 6× loading dye; 5 minutes.
12. When the cycling finishes, spin the tubes down and add 5 µL of loading dye to each; 5 minutes.
13. Load 10 µL per well alongside 5 µL of ladder; 8 minutes. Nothing goes into a well until the gel is in the rig and the ladder is ready.
14. Run the gel at 120 V for 40 minutes, until the dye front is two-thirds down.
15. Image the gel on the transilluminator; 5 minutes.
16. Record which clones carry the insert and mark the plate; 10 minutes.
>>>

Read all of it before you answer. Then say back, in one paragraph and in your own words: what is being made, for how many (or at what scale), by when, and under what constraints — equipment that exists only once, how many people are working, anything that has to be held, rested or ready at a particular moment. If the text you were given looks truncated, or points at a section that is not here, say so instead of filling the gap.

End your reply with the same read-back as JSON in a single ```json fenced block:


This is a colony PCR screen: one person takes eight candidate clones (nine 25 µL reactions, counting the spare) from thawed reagents through a 1 h 50 min thermocycler program and then onto a single agarose gel, reading the result off a transilluminator to decide which clones carry the insert. There is no stated clock time to hit — the instruction is simply to finish as early as the work honestly allows, with no rushes that would damage the gel. Everything is serialised through one operator and one of each shared instrument: thermocycler, microcentrifuge, microwave, gel rig and transilluminator. The main scheduling constraint is the deliberate overlap in the source text: the agarose gel is started 25 minutes *into* the cycling run, not after it, so the microwave/cool/pour/set/combo-removal work hides inside the 1 h 50 min block — but the 35-minute set must not be rushed, and the ladder is thawed ten minutes after the pour. Two hard holds: the polymerase stays in the cold block until the last moment of master-mix assembly, and nothing goes into a well until the gel is seated in the rig under TAE *and* the ladder is ready. The single 10-well comb also means one gel's worth of lanes for eight clones plus ladder, so the load step (10 µL sample + 5 µL ladder) is a single bottleneck, and the whole run then waits on 40 minutes at 120 V before imaging and 10 minutes of plate marking. Nothing in the text appears truncated; parts 1–4, steps 1–16, are all present.

While cycling runs, an agarose gel is started 25 minutes in - weigh, microwave 3 min, cool 12 min, add stain and pour into one casting tray with a 10-well comb, set 35 unhurried minutes, then de-comb into the rig under 1x TAE; the 100 bp ladder is thawed 10 minutes after the pour. When cycling ends the tubes are spun and dyed, loaded 10 uL per well plus 5 uL ladder (nothing enters a well until the gel is in the rig and the ladder is ready), run 40 min at 120 V, imaged on the transilluminator and the plate marked to record which clones carry the insert. No deadline was given; the goal is the earliest finish the work allows. **The model, in my own words.** A **track** is one sequential line of work — a station, an instrument or a performer — and the steps inside it never overlap, so anything that must happen *while* something else is running lives in a different track. Each **step** has exactly one duration kind: `fixed` with `seconds`, `variable` with `minSeconds`/`maxSeconds` (plus `defaultSeconds` so previews plan sensibly), or `indefinite`, which runs until the operator ends it. A **startTrigger** is how a step joins the clock or another step: `programStart`, `programStartOffset`, `afterStep`, `afterStepWithBuffer`, `manual`, `onAbort`, or a `compound` of several — with an optional `offsetSeconds`/`bufferSeconds` and an `instances` clause for replicated upstreams. **stepId**s are unique across the whole program, not per track, and every `task` a step occupies needs a matching **resourceConstraints** entry whose `maxConcurrent` is what actually stops two steps sharing the one thermocycler, the one centrifuge or the one operator. Repeated work is a single `replicates: {count, mode}` step rather than hand-copied steps, chained forward with `instances: "each"`, collapsed by an `instances: "all"` barrier, and throttled by `replicates.maxInFlight: k` when the holding area between repetitions only fits k. Tracks are where I'll put *parallel* work (cycling vs. gel casting), triggers are how I'll express the "start the gel 25 minutes into the run" overlap, and constraints will carry the single-instance bench.

**What I expect to declare.** Six of these are named in the source: thermocycler, microcentrifuge, microwave, gel rig, transilluminator — plus the one operator, who is the real bottleneck and who I want modelled as a task claimed by hands-on steps (an `actors: 1` program, but explicit is safer for the validator). I add the **cold block / ice** because the polymerase is deliberately parked there until master-mix assembly, and a **bench/prep** surface for pipetting and for the 12-minute flask cooling and 35-minute set, which occupy space rather than an instrument. Nothing here is replicated — eight clones are eight reactions, but they are assembled as *one* master mix and loaded as *one* 10 µL-per-well gel, so no `replicates`, no holding area, no `maxInFlight`; the single 10-well comb is a plain bottleneck, not a WIP cap.
